blocks.x: Myiasis is the infection of fly larvae (maggots) in human tissue, such as skin. It occurs mainly in tropical and subtropical areas, and people with untreated, open wounds are at greater risk.
Four genera behind most human cases

items: A lump develops in tissue as the larva grows.
Larvae under the skin may move on occasion.
Usually, larvae remain under the skin and do not travel throughout the body.

sections.title: The human bot fly, in detail

blocks.x: The human bot fly has one of the most unusual life cycles in medical entomology: it doesn't lay its eggs directly on a host, but hijacks a blood-sucking insect to deliver them.

blocks.cap: Life cycle diagram of Dermatobia hominis showing adult, eggs laid on a blood-sucking vector, larvae entering the host, larva under the skin, pupa in soil, and back to adult
Close-up photographs of Dermatobia hominis larvae removed from a human host, showing the whole larvae, the anterior end with mandibles, and the posterior end
Photographs comparing adult flies known to cause myiasis in humans: Dermatobia hominis, Cochliomyia hominivorax, and Cuterebra species

items: Infestations are often characterised by cutaneous swellings on the body or scalp that may produce discharges and be painful.
Death is rare, but there have been instances of cerebral myiasis in children, where larvae enter the brain.
Diagnosis is made by finding fly larvae in tissue.
Identification to genus or species level involves comparing morphological structures on the larvae.
Travel history can also help with genus- or species-level identification.

sections.title: Three ways larvae reach human tissue

blocks.x: Not every myiasis-causing fly behaves like Dermatobia hominis. Different species have evolved distinct strategies for getting their larvae onto — and into — a host.

sections.title: The fly families — and how myiasis is classified

blocks.x: Three fly families account for most economically important myiasis in livestock and humans, and cases themselves are grouped by how dependent the fly is on a living host.
Once larvae are confirmed in tissue, management focuses on safe removal and preventing complications; prevention centres on reducing contact between skin, wounds and egg-laying flies.
